claim: Perception and cognition are modulated by the phase of the cardiac signal in which the stimuli are presented.
source: Perception and cognition are modulated by the phase of the cardiac signal in which the stimuli are presented.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract supported by citations in the introduction to previous research.

claim: Touches initiated in the systole phase were held for longer periods of time than touches initiated in the diastole phase.
source: Touches initiated in the systole phase were held for longer periods of time than touches initiated in the diastole phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: The effect of longer touch duration in systole was most pronounced when elongating the duration of the touches to sense the most difficult gratings.
source: This effect was most pronounced when elongating the duration of the touches to sense the most difficult gratings.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis showing interaction with task difficulty and touch variability.

claim: While touches in the control condition were coupled to the cardiac cycle, their length did not vary as a function of the phase in which these were initiated.
source: Conversely, while touches in the control condition were coupled to the cardiac cycle, their length did not vary as a function of the phase in which these were initiated.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis showing no significant difference in touch duration by cardiac phase in the control condition.

claim: We actively spend more time sensing during systole periods, the cardiac phase associated with lower perceptual sensitivity.
source: Our results reveal that we actively spend more time sensing during systole periods, the cardiac phase associated with lower perceptual sensitivity (vs. diastole).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing longer touch durations when initiated in systole.

claim: We actively adjust the acquisition of sense data to our internal bodily cycles.
source: In line with interoceptive inference accounts, these results indicate that we actively adjust the acquisition of sense data to our internal bodily cycles.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results in the context of interoceptive inference theory.

claim: Active touch refers to what is ordinarily called touching (vs. passive touch, or being touched).
source: This notion was already noted by Gibson, 1962, who in the context of active sensing proposed that active touch refers to what is ordinarily called touching (vs. passive touch, or being touched).
evidence: This claim is attributed to Gibson, 1962 through citation.

claim: Active touch is built upon the processing of our own body in space and the stimuli in our environment, that is, proprioception and exteroception.
source: Also, he proposed that active touch is built upon the processing of our own body in space and the stimuli in our environment, that is, proprioception and exteroception.
evidence: This is attributed to Gibson's proposal through citation.

claim: Sensations depend on the internal state of the body when the stimuli are processed (i.e., interoception).
source: Yet, it is now well established that sensations also depend on the internal state of the body when the stimuli are processed (i.e., interoception; Al et al., 2020; Azzalini et al., 2019; Galvez-Pol et al., 2020a; Garfinkel et al., 2014; Khalsa et al., 2018; Quigley et al., 2021; Salomon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The heart has two phases: in the systole phase the heart ejects the blood, whereas in the diastole phase it refills.
source: As an intrinsic oscillator, the heart has two phases: in the systole phase the heart ejects the blood, whereas in the diastole phase it refills.
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge about cardiac function.

claim: Perceptual sensitivity to painful, visual, tactile, and auditory stimuli are typically reduced when they are presented in systole compared with diastole.
source: Perceptual sensitivity to painful, visual, tactile, and auditory stimuli are typically reduced when they are presented in systole compared with diastole (Al et al., 2020; Edwards et al., 2001; Edwards et al., 2007; Grund et al., 2022; McIntyre et al., 2006; Motyka et al., 2019; Pramme et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: These effects reflect cardiac-related sensory attenuation due to the competing allocation of attentional resources during periods of afferent signalling from the baroreceptors in systole.
source: It has been proposed that these effects reflect cardiac-related sensory attenuation due to the competing allocation of attentional resources (Berntson and Khalsa, 2021; Critchley and Garfinkel, 2018; Khalsa et al., 2018) during periods of afferent signalling from the baroreceptors in systole (Critchley and Harrison, 2013; Garfinkel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations.

claim: Saccades and visual fixations are coupled to the systole and diastole phases of the cardiac cycle.
source: In this context, we have recently shown that in an active sampling visual paradigm, saccades, and visual fixations are coupled to the systole and diastole phases of the cardiac cycle (Galvez-Pol et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: 46 participants performed the active tactile discrimination task.
source: To test these hypotheses, 46 participants performed the active tactile discrimination task illustrated in Figure 1.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: The proportion of rejected trials comprised 5.5% of the total number of trials, standard deviation (SD) = 4% across participants.
source: The proportion of rejected trials (see Methods) comprised 5.5% of the total number of trials, standard deviation (SD) = 4% across participants.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the experimental data.

claim: The mean number of computed heartbeats during participants' touch was 540, SD = ±173.
source: The mean number of computed heartbeats during participants' touch was 540, SD = ±173.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the experimental data.

claim: Participants' mean heart rate was 76 bpm, with a mean time between R-peaks of 793 ms and SD = ±110 ms.
source: Participants' mean heart rate was 76 bpm, with a mean time between R-peaks of 793 ms and SD = ±110 ms.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the experimental data.

claim: The percentage of correct responses was 82.7%, SD ± 6.6%.
source: The percentage of correct responses was 82.7%, SD ± 6.6%, and the mean duration of participants' touch in the whole experiment was 1103 ms, SD = 457.40 ms, Mdn = 999 ms.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the experimental data.

claim: The mean duration of participants' touch in the whole experiment was 1103 ms, SD = 457.40 ms, Mdn = 999 ms.
source: The percentage of correct responses was 82.7%, SD ± 6.6%, and the mean duration of participants' touch in the whole experiment was 1103 ms, SD = 457.40 ms, Mdn = 999 ms.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the experimental data.

claim: The mean duration of the systole phase was 342 ms and the SD = 23.4 ms.
source: The mean duration of the systole phase was 342 ms and the SD = 23.4 ms, which is the expected duration for the mean heart rate of our sample (Mao et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the experimental data, validated by citation.

claim: There was a significant effect of task difficulty on participants' performance (F(3.34, 150) = 154, p < 0.0001, ηp2 = 0.774).
source: This analysis showed a significant effect of task difficulty on participants' performance (F(3.34, 150) = 154, p < 0.0001, ηp2 = 0.774).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: Participants' performance for the first four levels of difficulty was fairly similar (all p > 0.086).
source: Post hoc comparisons showed that participants' performance for the first four levels of difficulty was fairly similar (all p > 0.086; see Supplementary file 1A, B for all post hoc comparisons).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc comparisons.

claim: Performance in the first four difficulty levels was significantly greater than in the remaining levels of difficulty (all p < 0.0001, d > 0.833).
source: Yet, performance in these levels was significantly greater than in the remaining levels of difficulty (all p < 0.0001, d > 0.833).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc comparisons.

claim: The proportion of correct responses in difficulty level 5 was significantly greater than those in difficulty levels 6 and 7 (both p < 0.0001, d > 1.618).
source: Likewise, the proportion of correct responses in difficulty level 5 was significantly greater than those in difficulty levels 6 and 7 (both p < 0.0001, d > 1.618; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc comparisons, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: There was a significant effect of task difficulty on the time spent holding the touch (F(1.70, 76.6) = 25.1, p < 0.0001, ηp2 = 0.358).
source: There was a significant effect of task difficulty on the time spent holding the touch (F(1.70, 76.6) = 25.1, p < 0.0001, ηp2 = 0.358).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: The length of holding time for the first four levels of difficulty was similar (all p > 0.065).
source: Post hoc comparisons showed that the length of holding time for the first four levels of difficulty was similar (all p > 0.065), as well as shorter than in the remaining levels of difficulty (all p < 0.01, d > −0.416).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc comparisons.

claim: The holding time for the control movement condition (flat stimulus) was significantly shorter than for the gratings across all seven levels of difficulty (p ≤ 0.05, d > −0.416).
source: The results show that the holding time for the control movement condition (flat stimulus) was significantly shorter than for the gratings across all seven levels of difficulty (p ≤ 0.05, d > −0.416; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing conditions, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: The start of touches occurred on average during the first half of the cardiac cycle at 151°.
source: The start of touches occurred on average during the first half of the cardiac cycle at 151°.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from circular analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The phase of the initiation of touches in circular space did not differ significantly from a uniform distribution (Rayleigh test z = 0.134, p = 0.44).
source: The phase of the initiation of touches in circular space did not differ significantly from a uniform distribution (Rayleigh test z = 0.134, p = 0.44; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from circular analysis, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: The mean phase of the holding touches occurred on average circa the mid part of the cycle at 202°.
source: The mean phase of the holding touches occurred on average circa the mid part of the cycle at 202°.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from circular analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The distribution of holding touches did not differ from uniformity (Rayleigh test z = 0.155, p = 0.331).
source: Their distribution did not differ from uniformity (Rayleigh test z = 0.155, p = 0.331).
evidence: This is a statistical result from circular analysis.

claim: The distribution of ending touches in circular space, which occurred on average during the latter part of the cycle at 278°, did not differ significantly from a uniform distribution (Rayleigh test z = 0.243, p = 0.065).
source: Likewise, the distribution of ending touches in circular space, which occurred on average during the latter part of the cycle at 278°, did not differ significantly from a uniform distribution (Rayleigh test z = 0.243, p = 0.065).
evidence: This is a statistical result from circular analysis.

claim: In the control movement condition, the start of the touches occurred on average during the first half of the heartbeats at 101°.
source: In the control movement condition, the start of the touches occurred on average during the first half of the heartbeats at 101°.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from circular analysis of the control condition data.

claim: The distribution of touch starts in the control condition differed significantly from a uniform distribution (Rayleigh test z = 0.267, p = 0.039).
source: The distribution of these touches differed significantly from a uniform distribution (Rayleigh test z = 0.267, p = 0.039; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a statistical result from circular analysis, with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: In the control condition, the holding of touches occurred on average during the mid-part of the cycle at 168° and their distribution differed significantly from a uniform distribution (Rayleigh test z = 0.316, p = 0.010).
source: Regarding the holding of touches, they occurred on average during the mid-part of the cycle at 168° and their distribution differed significantly from a uniform distribution (Rayleigh test z = 0.316, p = 0.010).
evidence: This is a statistical result from circular analysis of the control condition.

claim: In the control condition, the end of touches occurred on average during the second half of the heartbeats at 243° and the distribution was marginally different from a uniform distribution (Rayleigh test z = 0.260, p = 0.046).
source: Last, the end of touches occurred on average during the second half of the heartbeats at 243°. The distribution was marginally different from a uniform distribution (Rayleigh test z = 0.260, p = 0.046).
evidence: This is a statistical result from circular analysis of the control condition.

claim: Active touches were coupled with the cardiac cycle in the control movement condition.
source: These results indicate that active touches were coupled with the cardiac cycle in the control movement condition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical results showing non-uniform distributions.

claim: There was a significant main effect of event type on the proportion of touches in systole vs. diastole (F(1, 44) = 9.91, p = 0.003, ηp2 = 0.184).
source: This analysis showed a significant main effect of event type (F(1, 44) = 9.91, p = 0.003, ηp2 = 0.184), a non-significant effect of experimental condition (F(1, 44) = 0.47, p = 0.499, ηp2 = 0.010), and a non-significant interaction between both variables (F(1, 44) = 4.04, p = 0.051, ηp2 = 0.084).
evidence: This is a statistical result from rmANOVA analysis.

claim: For the gratings, the proportion of touches that started in systole was significantly greater than the proportion of touches that ended in systole (t(45) = −2.22, p = 0.032, d = −0.327, 95% CI mean difference [−0.040, −0.002]).
source: For the gratings, the proportion of touches that started in systole was significantly greater than the proportion of touches that ended in systole (t(45) = −2.22, p = 0.032, d = −0.327, 95% confidence interval [CI] mean difference [−0.040, −0.002]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from t-test analysis.

claim: In the control movement condition, the proportion of touches that started in systole was significantly greater than that of touches that ended in systole (t(44) = −2.75, p = 0.009, d = −0.410, 95% CI mean difference [−0.125, −0.019]).
source: Likewise, in the control movement condition, the proportion of touches that started in systole was significantly greater than that of touches that ended in systole (t(44) = −2.75, p = 0.009, d = −0.410, 95% CI mean difference [−0.125, −0.019]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from t-test analysis.

claim: For the gratings condition, the proportion of touches starting in systole did not differ from chance level (F(1, 45) = 0.19, p = 0.662, ηp2 = 0.004).
source: For the gratings condition, the proportion of touches starting in systole did not differ from chance level (F(1, 45) = 0.19, p = 0.662, ηp2 = 0.004).
evidence: This is a statistical result from one-sample test.

claim: For the gratings condition, the proportion of touches ending in systole was significantly smaller than chance level (F(1, 45) = 6.33, p = 0.015, ηp2 = 0.123).
source: In contrast, the proportion of touches ending in systole was significantly smaller than chance level (F(1, 45) = 6.33, p = 0.015, ηp2 = 0.123).
evidence: This is a statistical result from one-sample test.

claim: In the control movement condition, the proportion of touches starting in systole did not differ from chance level (t(44) = 1.18, p = 0.244, d = 0.176, 95% CI mean difference [−0.015, 0.058]).
source: Similarly, in the control movement condition the proportion of touches starting in systole did not differ from chance level (t(44) = 1.18, p = 0.244, d = 0.176, 95% CI mean difference [−0.015, 0.058]), whereas the proportion of touches ending in systole was significantly smaller than chance level (t(44) = −3.67, p = 0.0007, d = −0.547, 95% CI mean difference [−0.079, −0.023]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from one-sample t-test.

claim: In the control movement condition, the proportion of touches ending in systole was significantly smaller than chance level (t(44) = −3.67, p = 0.0007, d = −0.547, 95% CI mean difference [−0.079, −0.023]).
source: Similarly, in the control movement condition the proportion of touches starting in systole did not differ from chance level (t(44) = 1.18, p = 0.244, d = 0.176, 95% CI mean difference [−0.015, 0.058]), whereas the proportion of touches ending in systole was significantly smaller than chance level (t(44) = −3.67, p = 0.0007, d = −0.547, 95% CI mean difference [−0.079, −0.023]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from one-sample t-test.

claim: The proportion of touches starting and ending in each cardiac phase did not vary with task difficulty (F(6, 270) = 1.12, p = 0.349, ηp2 = 0.024) and (F(6, 270) = 0.69, p = 0.659, ηp2 = 0.015).
source: These analyses showed that the proportion of touches starting and ending in each cardiac phase did not vary with task difficulty (F(6, 270) = 1.12, p = 0.349, ηp2 = 0.024) and (F(6, 270) = 0.69, p = 0.659, ηp2 = 0.015).
evidence: This is a statistical result from one-way ANOVA.

claim: Participants were more likely to end the touch and subsequent sensing in the diastole phase of the cardiac cycle.
source: However, they were more likely to end the touch and subsequent sensing in the diastole phase of the cardiac cycle.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding that fewer touches ended in systole than chance.

claim: Regardless of the cardiac phase in which the touches were generated, participants were equally correct in their responses.
source: Overall, these results show that regardless of the cardiac phase in which the touches were generated, our participants were equally correct in their responses (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the rmANOVA showing no significant effects of cardiac phase on correct responses, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: The effect of cardiac phase on correct responses was not significant (F(1, 45) = 1.40, p = 0.243, ηp2 = 0.03).
source: This analysis showed that the effect of cardiac phase (F(1, 45) = 1.40, p = 0.243, ηp2 = 0.03), the effect of event type (F(1, 45) = 1.71, p = 0.198, ηp2 = 0.04), and all interactions between these variables were not significant (p > 0.340).
evidence: This is a statistical result from rmANOVA.

claim: For the gratings condition, the duration of touches initiated in systole 1143 ms (SD = 486.6) was greater than when touches were initiated in diastole 1093 ms (SD = 443.4), z = 855, p = 0.0004, r = 0.582, 95% CI mean difference [18.11, 71.18].
source: Hence, we used a Wilcoxon signed-rank test to show that the duration of touches initiated in systole 1143 ms (SD = 486.6) was greater than when touches were initiated in diastole 1093 ms (SD = 443.4), z = 855, p = 0.0004, r = 0.582, 95% CI mean difference [18.11, 71.18], Figure 3C.
evidence: This is a statistical result from Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: For the control movement condition, the duration of touches initiated in systole (M = 708, SD = 441.7) and diastole (M = 717, SD = 429.4) showed no differences, z = 461.5, p = 0.531, r = −0.108, 95% CI mean difference [−25.25, 13.50].
source: For the control movement condition, the equivalent analysis showed no differences in the duration of touches initiated in systole (M = 708, SD = 441.7) and diastole (M = 717, SD = 429.4), z = 461.5, p = 0.531, r = −0.108, 95% CI mean difference [−25.25, 13.50], Figure 3D.
evidence: This is a statistical result from Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: The duration of touches varied as a function of the cardiac phase in which these were initiated.
source: Overall, these results demonstrate that the duration of touches varied as a function of the cardiac phase in which these were initiated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analyses showing differences in touch duration by cardiac phase.

claim: Touches initiated in systole were longer than those initiated in diastole.
source: Touches initiated in systole were longer than those initiated in diastole.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental finding.

claim: Tactile sensitivity is greater in diastole than in systole.
source: Given that tactile sensitivity is greater in diastole than in systole (see e.g., Al et al., 2021a), these results suggest that our participants overcome the less sensitive phase (systole) through the elongation of the holding touch beyond this phase.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Participants overcome the less sensitive phase (systole) through the elongation of the holding touch beyond this phase.
source: Given that tactile sensitivity is greater in diastole than in systole (see e.g., Al et al., 2021a), these results suggest that our participants overcome the less sensitive phase (systole) through the elongation of the holding touch beyond this phase.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data combined with previous research.

claim: This modulation was only observed when tactile discrimination was required.
source: Furthermore, and importantly, this modulation was only observed when tactile discrimination was required.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the gratings and control conditions.

claim: There was a significant interaction between task difficulty and touch variability (F(2.909, 127.993) = 41.706, p < 0.0001, ηp2 = 0.487).
source: In addition, there was a significant interaction between task difficulty and touch variability (F(2.909, 127.993) = 41.706, p < 0.0001, ηp2 = 0.487), a significant interaction between cardiac phase and touch variability (F(1, 44) = 17.728, p = 0.0001, ηp2 = 0.287), and a significant interaction between task difficulty, cardiac phase, and touch variability (F(4.089, 179.904) = 4.239, p = 0.002, ηp2 = 0.088).
evidence: This is a statistical result from rmANOVA with touch variability as covariate.

claim: There was a significant interaction between cardiac phase and touch variability (F(1, 44) = 17.728, p = 0.0001, ηp2 = 0.287).
source: In addition, there was a significant interaction between task difficulty and touch variability (F(2.909, 127.993) = 41.706, p < 0.0001, ηp2 = 0.487), a significant interaction between cardiac phase and touch variability (F(1, 44) = 17.728, p = 0.0001, ηp2 = 0.287), and a significant interaction between task difficulty, cardiac phase, and touch variability (F(4.089, 179.904) = 4.239, p = 0.002, ηp2 = 0.088).
evidence: This is a statistical result from rmANOVA with touch variability as covariate.

claim: There was a significant interaction between task difficulty, cardiac phase, and touch variability (F(4.089, 179.904) = 4.239, p = 0.002, ηp2 = 0.088).
source: In addition, there was a significant interaction between task difficulty and touch variability (F(2.909, 127.993) = 41.706, p < 0.0001, ηp2 = 0.487), a significant interaction between cardiac phase and touch variability (F(1, 44) = 17.728, p = 0.0001, ηp2 = 0.287), and a significant interaction between task difficulty, cardiac phase, and touch variability (F(4.089, 179.904) = 4.239, p = 0.002, ηp2 = 0.088).
evidence: This is a statistical result from rmANOVA with touch variability as covariate.

claim: The correlation between participants' correct responses and the variability in the duration of their touches was significant (Pearson's r = 0.387, p = 0.008).
source: In addition, the correlation between participants' correct responses and the variability in the duration of their touches was significant (Pearson's r = 0.387, p = 0.008; Supplementary file 1) indicating that participants who varied the duration of their stationary holds in the experiment were also those with greater tactile discrimination performance.
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis.

claim: Participants who varied the duration of their stationary holds in the experiment were also those with greater tactile discrimination performance.
source: In addition, the correlation between participants' correct responses and the variability in the duration of their touches was significant (Pearson's r = 0.387, p = 0.008; Supplementary file 1) indicating that participants who varied the duration of their stationary holds in the experiment were also those with greater tactile discrimination performance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation result.

claim: Touches initiated in systole were held for longer periods (vs. touches initiated in diastole), and this cardiac-related modulation was particularly exhibited by those participants who varied the duration of their touches when sampling the most difficult gratings.
source: Overall, these results demonstrate that touches initiated in systole were held for longer periods (vs. touches initiated in diastole). This cardiac-related modulation was particularly exhibited by those participants who varied the duration of their touches when sampling the most difficult gratings (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis with touch variability as covariate, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: For the gratings condition, there was a significant main effect of heartbeat position on the duration of the IBIs (F(2.062, 92.788) = 11.65, p < 0.0001, ηp2 = 0.206).
source: In the gratings condition, there was a significant main effect of heartbeat position on the duration of the IBIs (F(2.062, 92.788) = 11.65, p < 0.0001, ηp2 = 0.206).
evidence: This is a statistical result from rmANOVA.

claim: The duration of the IBI in the starting touch (M = 797.8, SD = 111.7) was significantly longer than in the remaining heartbeats (all p < 0.006, all d > 0.502).
source: Post hoc comparisons showed that the duration of the IBI in the starting touch (M = 797.8, SD = 111.7) was significantly longer than in the remaining heartbeats (all p < 0.006, all d > 0.502; M − 2 = 784.2, M − 1 = 789.9, M + 1 = 789.8, M + 2 = 783.7; adjusted for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc comparisons.

claim: For the control movement condition, there was a significant main effect of heartbeat position on the duration of the IBIs (F(2.595, 114.201) = 10.75, p < 0.0001, ηp2 = 0.196).
source: For the control movement condition, the results also show a significant main effect of heartbeat position on the duration of the IBIs F(2.595, 114.201) = 10.75, p < 0.0001, ηp2 = 0.196.
evidence: This is a statistical result from rmANOVA.

claim: For the control movement condition, the duration of the IBI in the starting touch (M = 821.4, SD = 118.6) was significantly longer than in the two previous heartbeats (all p < 0.015, all d > 0.473).
source: Post hoc comparisons revealed that the duration of the IBI in the starting touch (M = 821.4, SD = 118.6) was significantly longer than in the two previous heartbeats (all p < 0.015, all d > 0.473; M − 2 = 802.5, M − 1 = 810.6).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc comparisons.

claim: For both stimulus conditions, the duration of systole in the preceding and successive heartbeats (relative to the starting touch) did not change (p > 0.235, ηp2 < 0.032).
source: The results showed that for both stimulus conditions, the duration of systole in the preceding and successive heartbeats (relative to the staring touch) did not change (p > 0.235, ηp2 < 0.032).
evidence: This is a statistical result from analysis of systole duration.

claim: For the diastole phase, the analyses showed a significant main effect of heartbeat position (p < 0.0001, ηp2 > 0.200).
source: Conversely, for the diastole phase, the analyses showed a significant main effect of heartbeat position (p < 0.0001, ηp2 > 0.200).
evidence: This is a statistical result from analysis of diastole duration.

claim: The changes observed in the whole IBIs were due to variations in the diastole phase.
source: The post hoc analysis revealed that the changes that we observed in the whole IBIs were due to variations in the diastole phase (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is a conclusion from post hoc analysis, with reference to Figure 5A, B.

claim: Changes in the duration of the cardiac cycle are due to the lengthening and compression of the diastole phase (relative to touch onset).
source: Moreover, our results show that changes in the duration of the cardiac cycle are due to the lengthening and compression of the diastole phase (relative to touch onset).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of systole and diastole durations.

claim: The lengthening of the diastole phase during active sensing touch might aid performance.
source: The lengthening of the diastole phase during active sensing touch might aid performance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The results confirm the deacceleration of the cardiac cycle in anticipation or reaction to salient stimuli and the later acceleration after the implementation of a response.
source: These results confirm the deacceleration of the cardiac cycle in anticipation or reaction to salient stimuli and the later acceleration after the implementation of a response (Lacey and Lacey, 1977; Sandman et al., 1977; Coles and Duncan-Johnson, 1975; Park et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the current data and citations to previous research.

claim: During the systole phase of the cardiac cycle, pressure sensors located in the carotid sinus, coronary arteries, and aortic arch (baroreceptors), detect changes in blood pressure and convey the strength and timing of heartbeats to the brainstem through the vagus nerve.
source: During the systole phase of the cardiac cycle, pressure sensors located in the carotid sinus, coronary arteries, and aortic arch (baroreceptors), detect changes in blood pressure and convey the strength and timing of heartbeats to the brainstem through the vagus nerve (Critchley and Harrison, 2013; Davos et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The arterial baroreflex system through variations in heart rate, vascular tone, and stroke volume, buffers blood pressure fluctuations.
source: Then, the arterial baroreflex system through variations in heart rate, vascular tone, and stroke volume, buffers blood pressure fluctuations (Vaschillo et al., 2011; Vaschillo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The ejected blood exerts pulsations with a direct effect on muscle activity.
source: Simultaneously, the ejected blood exerts pulsations with a direct effect on muscle activity (Birznieks et al., 2012; Fallon et al., 2004), eliciting small head and eye movements (Debener et al., 2010; Galvez-Pol et al., 2022; Lauridsen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The ejected blood elicits small head and eye movements.
source: Simultaneously, the ejected blood exerts pulsations with a direct effect on muscle activity (Birznieks et al., 2012; Fallon et al., 2004), eliciting small head and eye movements (Debener et al., 2010; Galvez-Pol et al., 2022; Lauridsen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.
